hook: Walter Pitts was born on April 23, 1923, in Detroit, Michigan, and taught himself logic as a boy after discovering Bertrand Russell and Alfred North Whitehead's Principia Mathematica in a public library, later corresponding with Russell directly. He left an unstable home as a teenager and eventually made his way to Chicago, where he met neurophysiologist Warren McCulloch through fellow researcher Jerome Lettvin. Working together, McCulloch and Pitts published A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity in 1943, showing that networks of simplified all-or-none neurons could compute any expression describable in formal logic, the first mathematical model of a neural network. Pitts moved to MIT in 1943 to study under Norbert Wiener without ever having earned a high school diploma, and he became a central figure in the early cybernetics movement alongside McCulloch, Wiener and Lettvin. He died on May 14, 1969, in Cambridge, Massachusetts, having destroyed his unfinished dissertation and papers some years earlier after a rift within the group.

quick_facts: Born April 23, 1923, in Detroit, Michigan, and died May 14, 1969, in Cambridge, Massachusetts.
Taught himself formal logic as a child after reading Russell and Whitehead's Principia Mathematica.
Left home as a teenager and never completed a high school diploma or formal degree.
Co-authored A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity with Warren McCulloch in 1943.
Joined MIT in 1943 to work with Norbert Wiener and became part of the founding circle of cybernetics.
The McCulloch-Pitts neuron later influenced Frank Rosenblatt's perceptron and subsequent neural network research.

achievements.title: A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity (1943)
achievements.impact: Introduced the first mathematical model of a neuron as a logical, all-or-none unit, providing the conceptual basis for later artificial neural networks.

achievements.title: Foundational contributions to cybernetics
achievements.impact: Helped connect formal logic, neuroscience and early computing within the Macy Conferences circle, shaping the interdisciplinary study of information processing in brains and machines.

achievements.title: Work with Jerome Lettvin and Warren McCulloch on visual perception
achievements.impact: Contributed mathematical formalism to frog vision research at MIT that influenced the study of neural coding.
